claim: Working memory deficits are present in many neuropsychiatric diseases with diagnosis-related severity.
source: Working memory deficits are present in many neuropsychiatric diseases with diagnosis-related severity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about working memory deficits across psychiatric diseases.

claim: A prediction model was built for letter three-back task performance in healthy participants using resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI).
source: We built a quantitative model for letter three-back task performance in healthy participants, using resting state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI).
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the construction of a prediction model using rs-fMRI data.

claim: The normative model was applied to independent participants (N = 965) including four psychiatric diagnoses.
source: This normative model was applied to independent participants (N = 965) including four psychiatric diagnoses.
evidence: The abstract states the sample size and composition of the test dataset.

claim: Individual's predicted WMA significantly correlated with measured WMA in both healthy population and schizophrenia.
source: Individual's predicted WMA significantly correlated with a measured WMA in both healthy population and schizophrenia.
evidence: The abstract reports significant correlations between predicted and measured working memory ability.

claim: Predicted effect size estimates on WMA impairment were comparable to previous meta-analysis results.
source: Our predicted effect size estimates on WMA impairment were comparable to previous meta-analysis results.
evidence: The abstract states that predicted effect sizes matched those from meta-analyses.

claim: Working memory is a goal-directed active information maintenance and manipulation in mind, forming a foundation for diverse complex cognitive functions, learning, and emotion regulation.
source: Working memory is a goal-directed active information maintenance and manipulation in mind, forming a foundation for diverse complex cognitive functions, learning, and emotion regulation (Baddeley, 2003; Cowan, 2014; Etkin et al., 2015; Otto et al., 2013).
evidence: This definition is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: A range of psychiatric disorders commonly shows working memory deficits, although the severity of the deficits is dependent of psychiatric diagnosis.
source: A range of psychiatric disorders commonly shows working memory deficits, although the severity of the deficits is dependent of psychiatric diagnosis (Forbes et al., 2009; Lever et al., 2015; Millan et al., 2012; Snyder, 2014; Snyder et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Working memory emerges by coordinating multiple related processes from sensory perception, cognitive control, to motor action and thus requires close communication among widespread brain regions.
source: Working memory emerges by coordinating multiple related processes from sensory perception, cognitive control (e.g. updating, focused attention), to motor action and thus requires close communication among widespread brain regions (D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Eriksson et al., 2015; Nee et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2005; Postle, 2006; Rottschy et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim about the neural basis of working memory is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Functional connectivity quantifies how brain regions are temporally coordinated and is increasingly used to examine brain network architecture.
source: Functional connectivity (FC) quantifies how brain regions are temporally coordinated and is increasingly used to examine brain network architecture.
evidence: This is a definitional statement about functional connectivity based on established knowledge.

claim: Resting state FC has been associated with a wide range of individual traits.
source: Resting state (i.e. task-free) FC has been associated with a wide range of individual traits (Baldassarre et al., 2012; Dosenbach et al., 2010; Lewis et al., 2009; Seeley et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Whole-brain FC models have demonstrated that sets of functional connections across widespread brain regions can predict performance on cognitive tasks.
source: For example, whole-brain FC models have recently demonstrated that sets of functional connections across widespread brain regions can predict performance on cognitive tasks (Finn et al., 2015; Rosenberg et al., 2016; Smith et al., 2015; Yamashita et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Different psychiatric diagnoses are related to unique patterns of FC.
source: Functional connectivity has also provided insight into the biological basis of psychiatric disorders and shown that different diagnoses are related to unique patterns of FC (Baker et al., 2014; Harrison et al., 2009; Kaiser et al., 2015; Yahata et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: A whole-brain FC-based model has been shown to reliably predict autism spectrum disorder (ASD), as well as individual clinical scores.
source: For example, a whole-brain FC-based model has been shown to reliably predict autism spectrum disorder (ASD), as well as individual clinical scores (Emerson et al., 2017; Lake et al., 2018; Yahata et al., 2016), suggesting that FC disruption is quantitatively relevant to behavioral abnormality.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on ASD prediction.

claim: The ATR dataset consisted of 17 healthy participants aged 19-24 years old.
source: We used the ATR dataset (N = 17, age 19–24 years old) to develop a prediction model of working memory ability.
evidence: The Methods section explicitly describes the ATR dataset composition.

claim: Participants in the ATR dataset performed a letter 3-back task for about 25 sessions (80–90 min).
source: The participants performed a letter 3-back task for about 25 sessions (80–90 min).
evidence: The Methods section describes the task protocol.

claim: Working memory ability was quantified by estimating a learning plateau in the letter 3-back task.
source: Working memory ability was quantified by estimating a learning plateau in this task as follows.
evidence: The Methods section describes how working memory ability was measured.

claim: Network-level rather than node-level connectivity features were used to avoid overfitting to training samples.
source: We used network-level rather than node-level connectivity features to avoid overfitting to training samples (the curse of dimensionality).
evidence: The Methods section explains the rationale for using network-level features.

claim: FC values were calculated based on 18 whole-brain intrinsic networks of BrainMap ICA.
source: Specifically, we calculated FC values, based on 18 whole-brain intrinsic networks of BrainMap ICA (Laird et al., 2011), for pair-wise between-network (18 × 17/2 = 153) connections and within-network connections.
evidence: The Methods section describes the connectivity estimation approach with citation.

claim: ICC values for functional connectivity estimation were 0.34 ± 0.12 for BNU 1, 0.26 ± 0.18 for IACAS 1, and 0.21 ± 0.17 for Utah 1 datasets.
source: As a result, we obtained ICC values 0.34 ± 0.12 (range 0 to 0.65) for BNU 1, 0.26 ± 0.18 (range 0 to 0.66) for IACAS 1, and 0.21 ± 0.17 (range 0 to 0.59) for Utah one datasets.
evidence: The Results section reports ICC values from test-retest reliability analysis.

claim: The connectivity estimation methods yielded 'fair' reliability (0.2 < ICC ≤ 0.4) for the three datasets.
source: According to an interpretation criteria of ICC (Landis and Koch, 1977), our connectivity estimation methods yielded 'fair' reliability (0.2 < ICC ≤ 0.4) for the three datasets.
evidence: The Results section interprets ICC values using established criteria.

claim: Test-retest reliability of the connectivity estimation methods are comparable to other common connectivity estimation methods.
source: These results suggest that test-retest reliability of our methods are comparable to other common connectivity estimation methods (Birn et al., 2013; Noble et al., 2017).
evidence: The Results section compares reliability to previous studies.

claim: Individual letter 3-back learning plateaus were modeled as a linear weighted summation of automatically selected 16 functional connectivity values among 15 intrinsic networks.
source: Using sparse linear regression, individual letter 3-back learning plateaus were modeled as a linear weighted summation of automatically selected 16 functional connectivity values among 15 intrinsic networks (Figure 2).
evidence: The Results section describes the model structure with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The letter 3-back learning plateaus were positively correlated with three functional connectivity values (P1-P3) and negatively correlated with the remaining 13 connectivity values (N1-N13).
source: The letter 3-back learning plateaus were positively correlated with three functional connectivity values (P1-P3) and negatively correlated with the remaining 13 connectivity values (N1-N13).
evidence: The Results section describes the directionality of correlations in the model.

claim: There was no significant correlation between the predicted letter 3-back learning plateau and age (r = 0.21, p = 0.42), gender (r = 0.28, p = 0.28), or head motion (r = -0.37, p = 0.14).
source: We did not find a significant correlation between the predicted letter 3-back learning plateau and age (r = 0.21, p = 0.42), gender (r = 0.28, p = 0.28), or head motion (r = - 0.37, p = 0.14).
evidence: The Results section reports correlation analyses with potential confounds.

claim: The HCP dataset analysis was restricted to participants for whom all rs-fMRI, visual-object N-back, the NIH Toolbox list-sorting test, and Raven's progressive matrices were available (N = 474).
source: We restricted our analysis to participants for whom all rs-fMRI, visual-object N-back, the NIH Toolbox list-sorting test (Tulsky et al., 2014), and Raven's progressive matrices with 24 items (Bilker et al., 2012) were available (N = 474; 194 males, 5 year age ranges in the Open Access Data: 22–25, 26–30, 31–35 and 36 + years old).
evidence: The Methods section describes the HCP dataset inclusion criteria.

claim: The visual-object N-back task and the list-sorting test scores were positively correlated with general fluid intelligence (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = 0.46, p = 3.3 × 10-26; ρ = 0.32, p = 5.7×10−13, respectively).
source: Before the generalization test, we found that the visual-object N-back task and the list-sorting test scores were positively correlated with general fluid intelligence (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = 0.46, p = 3.3 × 10-26;ρ = 0.32, p = 5.7×10−13, respectively)
evidence: The Results section reports correlations between working memory measures and fluid intelligence.

claim: The visual-object N-back task and the list-sorting test scores were negatively correlated with average in-scanner head motion (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.24, p = 1.5 × 10-7; ρ = −0.12, p = 0.009).
source: and negatively correlated with average in-scanner head motion (Spearman's rank correlation ρ = −0.24, p = 1.5 × 10-7; ρ = −0.12, p = 0.009)
evidence: The Results section reports correlations between working memory measures and head motion.

claim: There was a significant partial correlation of the predicted working memory ability with the measured visual-object N-back scores (Spearman's rank partial correlation ρ = 0.11; p = 0.0072) while factoring out general fluid intelligence and head motion.
source: This revealed a significant partial correlation of the predicted working memory ability with the measured visual-object N-back scores (Spearman's rank partial correlation ρ = 0.11; p = 0.0072, Figure 3A)
evidence: The Results section reports significant partial correlation with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: There was a significant partial correlation of the predicted working memory ability with the measured list-sorting scores (Spearman's rank partial correlation ρ = 0.084; p = 0.034) while factoring out general fluid intelligence and head motion.
source: and with the measured list-sorting scores (Spearman's rank partial correlation ρ = 0.084; p = 0.034).
evidence: The Results section reports significant partial correlation with list-sorting scores.

claim: The model captures FC variations specific to working memory ability independently of general fluid intelligence and head motion.
source: The model captures FC variations specific to working memory ability independently of general fluid intelligence and head motion.
evidence: The Results section interprets the partial correlation results.

claim: The schizophrenia dataset included 58 patients and 60 age- and gender-matched controls.
source: The schizophrenia patients (N = 58) and their age- and gender-matched controls (N = 60) underwent a cognitive test battery the Japanese version of Brief Assessment of Cognition in Schizophrenia (BACS-J) (Kaneda et al., 2007).
evidence: The Methods section describes the schizophrenia dataset composition.

claim: In schizophrenia patients, the digit-sequencing scores correlated positively with composite BACS score excluding working memory (r = 0.61, p = 3.0 × 10−7), negatively with age (r = −0.36, p = 0.005), but not with head motion (r = −0.03, p = 0.83).
source: Before the model application, we found that the digit-sequencing scores correlated positively with composite BACS score excluding working memory (r = 0.61, p = 3.0 × 10−7), negatively with age (r = −0.36, p = 0.005), but not with head motion (r = −0.03, p = 0.83) as shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: The Results section reports correlations in the schizophrenia patient group.

claim: While controlling age and composite BACS score, the model predictions showed significant correlations with digit-sequencing scores in schizophrenia patients (ρ = 0.25, p = 0.033).
source: While controlling the age and the composite BACS score using a partial correlation analysis, the model predictions showed significant correlations with digit-sequencing scores (ρ = 0.25, p = 0.033, Figure 3B).
evidence: The Results section reports significant partial correlation in schizophrenia patients with reference to Figure 3B.

claim: In the full sample of SCZ patients and controls, while controlling age and composite BACS score, the model prediction is significantly correlated with the digit-sequencing score (ρ = 0.15, p = 0.048).
source: While controlling the age and the composite BACS score, a partial correlation analysis showed that the model prediction is significantly correlated with the digit-sequencing score (ρ = 0.15, p = 0.048).
evidence: The Results section reports significant partial correlation in the combined sample.

claim: The model captures FC variations that are specific to working memory ability independently of age or the composite BACS score.
source: Therefore, the model captures FC variations that are specific to working memory ability independently of age or the composite BACS score.
evidence: The Results section interprets the partial correlation results.

claim: Significant differences in the predicted working memory ability between patients and controls were identified only for SCZ patients (two-tailed t-test for SCZ group: t116 = −3.68, P = (3.5 × 10−4) x 4 = 0.0014, Bonferroni corrected).
source: Consequently, we identified significant differences in the predicted working memory ability between the patients and controls only for SCZ patients (two-tailed t-test for SCZ group: t116 = −3.68, P = (3.5 × 10−4) x 4 = 0.0014, Bonferroni corrected; Figure 4A).
evidence: The Results section reports significant group differences for schizophrenia with reference to Figure 4A.

claim: A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of diagnosis on the Z-score (F3,245 = 7.63, p = 6.8 × 10−5).
source: A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of diagnosis on the Z-score (F3,245 = 7.63, p = 6.8 × 10−5).
evidence: The Results section reports ANOVA results for diagnosis effects.

claim: The severity of the predicted impairment in SCZ patients was larger than all other diagnoses (post-hoc Holm's controlled t-test, adjusted p < 0.05).
source: The severity of the predicted impairment in SCZ patients was larger than all other diagnoses (post-hoc Holm's controlled t-test, adjusted p < 0.05).
evidence: The Results section reports post-hoc test results comparing diagnoses.

claim: The predicted working memory ability alteration was more negative in the order of SCZ, MDD, OCD, and ASD with effect sizes (Hedge's g) of −0.68, –0.29, −0.16, and 0.09, respectively.
source: The predicted working memory ability alteration was more negative in the order of SCZ, MDD, OCD, and ASD with effect sizes (Hedge's g) of −0.68, –0.29, −0.16, and 0.09, respectively.
evidence: The Results section reports effect sizes for each diagnosis.

claim: The effect sizes of the predicted working memory impairment fell within confidence intervals for forward digit-span in SCZ, MDD, and OCD and for backward digit-span in OCD.
source: The effect sizes of the predicted working memory impairment fell within confidence intervals for forward digit-span in SCZ, MDD, and OCD and for backward digit-span in OCD (Figure 4C).
evidence: The Results section compares predicted effect sizes to meta-analysis confidence intervals with reference to Figure 4C.

claim: The model capturing a normal range of variation in working memory ability reproduced not only the order but also the quantitative aspects of working memory deterioration across the four distinct diagnoses.
source: Therefore, the model capturing a normal range of variation in working memory ability reproduced not only the order but also the quantitative aspects of working memory deterioration across the four distinct diagnoses.
evidence: The Results section interprets the comparison with meta-analysis results.

claim: Previous studies generally showed little differences in verbal working memory ability between ASD and typically developed controls.
source: However, previous studies generally showed little differences in verbal working memory ability from typically developed controls (Koshino et al., 2005; Lever et al., 2015; Williams et al., 2005), consistent with the predictions of our model.
evidence: The Results section cites previous studies on ASD working memory.

claim: No significant differences in head motion between patients and their healthy controls were identified in any diagnosis (two-tailed t-tests, at largest t138 = 1.77, p > 0.080 observed in ASD group).
source: We identified no significant differences in head motion between patients and their healthy controls in any diagnosis (two-tailed t-tests, at largest t138 = 1.77, p > 0.080 observed in ASD group).
evidence: The Results section reports head motion comparisons across diagnoses.

claim: A two-way ANOVA revealed a significant main effect of diagnosis on Z-scores (p < 1.0 × 10−4).
source: We entered the Z-score in a two-way ANOVA with diagnosis as a between-participant factor and connection as a within-participant factor. We found a significant main effect of diagnosis (p < 1.0 × 10−4; Figure 5B).
evidence: The Results section reports ANOVA results for Z-scores with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: SCZ patients showed significantly more negative mean Z-scores across connections than the other diagnoses (post-hoc diagnosis-pair-wise comparisons, p < 0.05).
source: SCZ patients showed significantly more negative mean Z-scores across connections than the other diagnoses (post-hoc diagnosis-pair-wise comparisons, p < 0.05).
evidence: The Results section reports post-hoc comparison results for Z-scores.

claim: The global patterns of the working memory ability-related 16 connections in SCZ were more severely disrupted than the other three diagnoses.
source: This suggests that the global patterns of the working memory ability-related 16 connections in SCZ were more severely disrupted than the other three diagnoses.
evidence: The Results section interprets the Z-score findings.

claim: A significant interaction effect between diagnosis and connection was found in the Z-scores (p < 1.0 × 10−5).
source: We found a significant interaction effect between diagnosis and connection in the Z-scores (p < 1.0 × 10−5), suggesting that FC alterations at particular connections are diagnosis-dependent.
evidence: The Results section reports a significant interaction effect in the ANOVA.

claim: In seven connections, the Z-scores were significantly different among the four diagnoses (Q < 0.05, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected).
source: In seven connections (Figure 5C), the Z-scores were significantly different among the four diagnoses (Q < 0.05, false discovery rate (FDR) corrected), suggesting that these connections are differentially altered across the diagnoses.
evidence: The Results section reports FDR-corrected results for specific connections with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: No significant difference was found between the distributions of chi-square values for the model's 16 connections and other 155 connections (p = 0.30).
source: Consequently, we found no significant difference between the distributions (p = 0.30).
evidence: The Results section reports a non-significant Kolmogorov-Smirnov test result.

claim: Connectivity is altered at the working memory ability-related connections as well as the other connections.
source: This means that connectivity is altered at the working memory ability-related connections as well as the other connections (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The Results section interprets the chi-square distribution comparison.

claim: The four diagnoses commonly showed altered connectivity related to the fronto-parietal cluster.
source: The four diagnoses commonly showed altered connectivity related to the fronto-parietal cluster.
evidence: The Results section describes common connectivity alterations across diagnoses.

claim: The motor/visuospatial, audition/speech, and visual clusters are associated with lower working memory in schizophrenia and MDD.
source: The motor/visuospatial, audition/speech, and visual clusters are associated with lower working memory in schizophrenia and MDD.
evidence: The Results section describes diagnosis-specific connectivity alterations.

claim: The results provide the first evidence for a common whole-brain FC-WMA relationship across healthy populations and a range of psychiatric disorders.
source: Our results provide the first evidence for a common whole-brain FC-WMA relationship across healthy populations and a range of psychiatric disorders.
evidence: The Discussion section claims novelty of the findings.

claim: Working memory impairment in psychiatric disorders is a continuous deviation from a normal pattern while preserving the common relationship between brain-wide connectivity and working memory ability.
source: That is, our results support the idea that working memory impairment in psychiatric disorders is a continuous deviation from a normal pattern while preserving the common relationship between brain-wide connectivity and working memory ability.
evidence: The Discussion section interprets the overall findings.

claim: The model's generalizability to completely independent datasets is supported by rigorous methods.
source: Our model's generalizability to completely independent datasets is supported by rigorous methods.
evidence: The Discussion section evaluates the methodological rigor.

claim: Careful evaluation of working memory ability in 1500 trials devoting about 80–90 min enhanced measurement precision by reducing trial-by-trial variability at the individual participant level.
source: Also, our careful evaluation of working memory ability in 1500 trials devoting about 80–90 min enhanced measurement precision by reducing trial-by-trial variability at the individual participant level (Smith and Little, 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section explains how extensive testing improved measurement precision.

claim: Larger sample sizes do not always improve prediction accuracy.
source: We note that larger sample sizes do not really always improve prediction accuracy.
evidence: The Discussion section makes a general statement about sample size and prediction accuracy.

claim: A new prediction model of visual-object N-back score using the HCP dataset as training dataset (N = 474) failed to provide significant prediction even within the training samples (R2 = 0.005).
source: Using identical methods in our model construction, we developed a new prediction model of visual-object N-back score using the HCP dataset as a training dataset (N = 474). However, this model failed to provide significant prediction even within the training samples (R2 = 0.005).
evidence: The Discussion section reports results from an additional analysis.

claim: The HCP conducted the N-back task in a limited time (160 trials for each individual), which may be noisy to precisely characterize individual ability.
source: The HCP conducted the N-back task in a limited time (160 trials for each individual), which may be noisy to precisely characterize individual ability.
evidence: The Discussion section speculates about reasons for poor prediction in HCP training.

claim: The model's accuracy was comparable with a previous model of attention ability for an external test set (r ~ 0.3).
source: Our model's accuracy was comparable with their model of attention ability for an external test set (r ~ 0.3).
evidence: The Discussion section compares model accuracy to previous work.

claim: The two-stage approach, which builds a normative model and applies it to multiple diagnoses, is an effective technique to systematically compare neural substrates across multiple diagnoses.
source: Our proposed two-stage approach, which builds a normative model and applies it to multiple diagnoses, is an effective technique to systematically compare neural substrates across multiple diagnoses.
evidence: The Discussion section evaluates the methodological approach.

claim: Clinical measures of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were previously predicted by FC patterns that determine attention ability in healthy populations.
source: Clinical measures of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were previously predicted by FC patterns that determine attention ability in healthy populations (Rosenberg et al., 2016), suggesting common connectivity-cognition relationships across healthy and clinical populations.
evidence: The Discussion section cites previous work supporting the approach.

claim: The two-stage approach could potentially cluster multiple psychiatric disorders based on neurobiological measures and behaviors.
source: By coherently establishing FC-cognition relationships from normal to abnormal, our two-stage approach could potentially cluster multiple psychiatric disorders based on neurobiological measures and behaviors (Insel et al., 2010).
evidence: The Discussion section speculates about potential applications.

claim: Recent transdiagnostic studies of genomics indicate that some neurobiological changes are shared across psychiatric diagnoses.
source: Such neurobiological insights into behavioral abnormality are consistent with recent transdiagnostic studies of genomics (Cross-Disorder Group of the Psychiatric Genomics Consortium, 2013; O'Donovan and Owen, 2016; Plomin et al., 2009)
evidence: The Discussion section cites genomics studies supporting transdiagnostic findings.

claim: Recent transdiagnostic neuroimaging studies indicate that some neurobiological changes are shared across psychiatric diagnoses.
source: and neuroimaging (Clementz et al., 2016; Goodkind et al., 2015; Sheffield et al., 2017), which indicate that some neurobiological changes are shared across psychiatric diagnoses.
evidence: The Discussion section cites neuroimaging studies supporting transdiagnostic findings.

claim: Recent studies provide evidence indicating that models of attention and memory generalize to predict behavior in patients as well as in healthy populations.
source: Consistent with our results, recent studies provide evidences indicating that models of attention and memory generalize to predict behavior in patient as well as in healthy populations (Kessler et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2018; O'Halloran et al., 2018; Rosenberg et al., 2016).
evidence: The Discussion section cites recent studies supporting generalization of cognitive models.

claim: The four diagnoses commonly showed altered connections related to the fronto-parietal networks.
source: First, the four diagnoses commonly showed altered connections related to the fronto-parietal networks.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes findings about fronto-parietal network alterations.

claim: This finding supports a hypothesis that the executive control network regulates symptoms, and its dysregulation is a shared neural substrate across diagnostic categories.
source: This finding support a hypothesis that the executive control network regulates symptoms, and its dysregulation is a shared neural substrate across diagnostic categories (Cole et al., 2014; Smucny et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section interprets findings in the context of previous hypotheses.

claim: Visual and auditory networks were associated with lower working memory ability in schizophrenia and MDD.
source: Second, visual and auditory networks were associated with lower working memory ability in schizophrenia and MDD.
evidence: The Discussion section summarizes findings about sensory network alterations.

claim: These results are consistent with the hypothesis that cognitive function is disrupted regarding not only top-down executive control but also bottom-up sensory processes.
source: These two results are consistent with the hypothesis that cognitive function is disrupted regarding not only top-down executive control but also bottom-up sensory processes (Javitt, 2009).
evidence: The Discussion section interprets findings in the context of a previous hypothesis.

claim: A neurophysiological study has suggested contributions of motor and premotor neurons to encoding serial order of working memory.
source: Recently, a neurophysiological study has suggested contributions of motor and premotor neurons to encoding serial order of working memory (Carpenter et al., 2018).
evidence: The Discussion section cites a neurophysiological study.

claim: Alterations of connections related to the motor/visuospatial networks were associated with lower working memory ability in schizophrenia, MDD, and ASD.
source: This is consistent with our result that alterations of connections related to the motor/visuospatial networks were associated with lower working memory ability in schizophrenia, MDD, and ASD.
evidence: The Discussion section relates findings to previous neurophysiological work.

claim: The test-retest reliability of functional connectivity estimation methods was fair level (0.2 < ICC ≤ 0.4) according to an interpretation criteria of ICC.
source: The test-retest reliability of our functional connectivity estimation methods was fair level (0.2 < ICC ≤ 0.4) according to an interpretation criteria of ICC (Landis and Koch, 1977).
evidence: The Discussion section evaluates the reliability of the methods.

claim: A previous study on test-retest reliability of functional connectivity between 18 different brain regions reported similar ICC values (ICC ~0.2) when scan length was 6 to 15 min.
source: A previous study on test-retest reliability of functional connectivity between 18 different brain regions (Birn et al., 2013), reported similar ICC values (ICC ~0.2) when scan length was 6 to 15 min.
evidence: The Discussion section compares reliability to previous studies.

claim: Another previous study examined functional connectivity reliability using 268 regions from whole-brain and reported that 6 min of scan length yielded similar reliability (dependability coefficient ~0.2 to 0.4).
source: Another previous study examined functional connectivity reliability (Noble et al., 2017), using 268 regions from whole-brain, also reported that 6 min of scan length yielded similar reliability (dependability coefficient ~0.2 to 0.4).
evidence: The Discussion section compares reliability to another previous study.

claim: The BrainMap ICA paper reported that IC18 (left FPN) has greater functional relevance to working memory than IC15 (right FPN) based on meta-analyses of thousands of publications.
source: The BrainMap ICA paper (Laird et al., 2011) reported that IC18 (left FPN) has greater functional relevance to working memory than IC15 (right FPN) based on meta-analyses of thousands of publications.
evidence: The Discussion section cites the BrainMap ICA paper to explain lateralization.

claim: A meta-analysis on N-back task with different stimulus modality found monitoring of verbal stimuli was strongly associated with left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Moreover, a meta-analysis on N-back task with different stimulus modality (Owen et al., 2005) found monitoring of verbal stimuli was strongly associated with left ventrolateral prefrontal cortex (a part of left FPN), while monitoring of spatial locations activated right lateralized frontal and parietal regions.
evidence: The Discussion section cites a meta-analysis to explain lateralization.

claim: The left FPN would be expected to contribute more to the prediction model than the right FPN because the study used a letter 3-back task that requires encoding alphabet letters.
source: In the current study, we used a letter 3-back task that requires encoding alphabet letters, which are more related to word monitoring than location monitoring. Therefore, the left FPN would be expected to contribute more to our prediction model than the right FPN.
evidence: The Discussion section provides a logical explanation for lateralization based on task properties.

claim: The right FPN showed a substantial contribution to working memory via negative connectivity N2 and N3 (~20% contribution).
source: Although large portion of the model relies on the within-network connectivity of the left FPN (~34% contribution), the right FPN also showed a substantial contribution to working memory via negative connectivity N2 (connection with the midbrain network, please see Figure 2) and N3 (connection with the superior parietal network) (~20% contribution).
evidence: The Discussion section quantifies the contribution of right FPN with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The primary limitation of this study is the assumption that the model captures general capability of working memory not restricted to letter 3-back performance.
source: The primary limitation of this study is the assumption that our model captures general capability of working memory not restricted to letter 3-back performance.
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges a key limitation.

claim: Working memory is an umbrella term which involves multiple distinct sensory modalities and executive functions, and the empirical findings and theoretical conceptualization is still rapidly extending.
source: Working memory is an umbrella term which involves multiple distinct sensory modalities and executive functions, and the empirical findings and theoretical conceptualization is still rapidly extending (Chatham and Badre, 2015; Cogan et al., 2017; D'Esposito and Postle, 2015; Ma et al., 2014; Myers et al., 2017; Serences, 2016).
evidence: The Discussion section describes the complexity of working memory with citations.

claim: Distinct types of working memory tasks are engaged with specific neural processes.
source: Future work may reveal more elaborate findings for FC-WMA relationships based on more nuanced definition of WMA, since distinct types of working memory tasks are engaged with specific neural processes (Nee et al., 2013; Owen et al., 2005).
evidence: The Discussion section suggests future directions with citations.

claim: Working memory performance was measured only in schizophrenia patients but not in other diagnostic groups.
source: Second, working memory performance was measured only in schizophrenia patients but not in other diagnostic groups.
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges a limitation in data availability.

claim: The participants are matched on age and sex within each site, but the groups may differ along a number of dimensions beyond working memory.
source: Third, although the participants are matched on age and sex within each site, the groups may differ along a number of dimensions beyond working memory (e.g. medication status, scanning protocol, and potentially IQ and other cognitive abilities).
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges potential confounds.

claim: Only a little variance can be explained by the model in the HCP dataset, which may be attributed to considerable differences between the HCP dataset and the ATR dataset.
source: Fourth, the results in the HCP dataset showed that only a little variance can be explained by our model. This may be attributed to considerable differences between the HCP dataset and the ATR dataset.
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges limited variance explained and speculates about reasons.

claim: In the HCP dataset, the model predictions were not more closely related to 2-back than 0-back performance.
source: Finally, in the HCP dataset, the model predictions were not more closely related to 2-back than 0-back performance.
evidence: The Discussion section acknowledges a limitation in task specificity.

claim: The model may capture abilities beyond working memory.
source: This result suggest that the model may capture abilities beyond working memory.

claim: The data provide a unified working memory ability framework across healthy populations and multiple psychiatric disorders.
